comment_text.value:
I think the definition of a reduction (in terms of what it buys) is allowed to be pretty much arbitrary while still having an effective distributed economy emerge on top of it. Think of it as a communist state that both issues currency, and sets arbitrary prices for all state-produced goods in terms of that currency. In one state, a loaf of bread (or a multiplication) might be worth $1, and a hamburger (or a network message send) $5; in another state, the costs might be reversed. This would shake out as

1. exchange rate nash-equilibria between dom0s, determined by their "monetary policies";

and 2. spawning of subagents on dom0s with better cost-structures for the particular tasks they're assigned to accomplish. (If you're doing a lot of network IO, you'd want to delegate that part of your job to a place where network IO—after currency-conversion—is cheap.)

comment_text.value:
> 2. Allocating bandwidth, storage, compute.

Before Bitcoin was a thing, I was thinking about the Erlang VM's "reduction-counting" processing paradigm, and noticed that it was a lot like having a dom0-scheduler "treasury" with domU-process "citizens", where each citizen gets paid a basic income every scheduling interval, and then can spend it to "purchase" time-spent-aware on a virtual core.

In Erlang's model, processes lose whatever they don't spend in a given interval—this is necessary to prevent a process from "saving up" and then blocking the VM for seconds at a time. However, if rather than putting a cap on wealth, you just cap spending per interval, then processes could do lots of other clever things with their income: trade it, invest it, spawn subagents that consume it, etc. This would be a very interesting platform for running goal-directed AI agents on: somewhere between Core Wars and Heroku.

Now, if the only "ledger" of reductions was in the local dom0, you'd have nothing more than a toy server: a sort of fishtank for agents to interact within. But throw a blockchain at the problem, and now agents could pay to spawn sub-agents (or copy themselves) anywhere that'll take their dom0's currency.

Interestingly, since cryptocoins are all pretty fungible, this would imply that the "intelligence" of an AI—or of a hypothetical Hansonian brain-emulation, for that matter—could be measured in units of dollars-spent-per-second.

comment_text.value:
Nice to see a gui coding agent. I use tui agents all the time but I am building a gui one. I use Claude Code, Codex, opencode and a couple other but I do not like the DX/UX.

I often want click a part of the wall of text (from agent) and search for related text, open them up on the side or so. I want to open a linked file. I want to answer multiple questions in an async manner, even come back and continue answering the next day.

There are many prompt level features I want too - orchestrate with subagents, but only the tasks I select - how do I select when there is no checkbox. Or maybe delegate a subagent to dig into (read only) one portion of the chat response. Maybe codify (write) only one task in a list of tasks. So many many other small things.

As a full-time user of coding agents, the TUI barely works for me. I think splitting text, searching in text, merging text are more important in agent driven development than ever before. It is all text, all the way. This is what I am building myself, with my own gui framework.

comment_text.value:
> What's useful about Herdr compared to tmux and claude code or codex's built in sub-agents?

Agent status detection. Single view over local and remote agents. /herdr skill that lets agents list other agents, peek into their panes, send keys (yes, you can make a lot of it work with tmux and some elbow grease, but herdr provides nice cli/api for it and works out of the box) including to remote ones.

In my mental model, subagents are also different from top level agents in tabs: subagents are only great as temporary workers you never want to interact with.

comment_text.value:
> Codex, Claude etc already do subagent management on their own

What about together? Can you reasonably do agent to agent interactions across harnesses? herdr makes that easy.

One of my favorite reasons for using herdr is what I'll call "everything is a pane". Running a new agent? Runs in a herdr pane. sshing into a system? Runs in a herdr pane. Anything that runs in a herdr pane, your agents can interact with. I will often do things like ssh into a system in one pane, and then ask pi in another pane to help me do diagnostics on that system. It never has to try to ssh in directly in the harness with my credentials, it just sends keyboard input to the pane, and reads the content of the pane. I can watch the interactive session as it goes by.

Another workflow that I have sometimes is I'll kick off some work in an agent, and instead of making a new sub agent, I'll actually make a new parent agent if I get worried that it's going down an unnecessary rabbit hole. I'll tell the new agent something like "periodically watch the agent in pane X, it is working on Y but I am concerned that it is losing track of its tasking. Periodically review what it's doing, and make sure it doesn't go off the rails. If it does seem to be going off the rails, give it guidance to bring it back on track" and that seems to have helped.

comment_text.value:
Claude Code's (CC) status summaries used 16.4% of our token spend in a week! We have investigated a source of overhead in CC: it's an agent_summary query that calls your current session/subagent model approximately every 30 seconds for a few words in CC’s status line.

Our DRIM system flagged the anomaly in CC's OTEL traces. Grouping requests by query_source showed that over one measured week agent_summary accounted for: 16.4% of total estimated spend (versus 15.7% for the main conversation), and 19.7% of all API requests with approximately 9,000 input tokens per output token.

Most requests reuse the prompt cache, but repeatedly reading a large cached transcript still has a cost. Longer contexts and more concurrent agents increase the overhead.

We couldn’t find a supported setting that disables only these summaries while preserving background agents and forks. Disabling those capabilities also stops the summaries, but changes the workflow we want to keep.

Our workaround is a small Bun preload that intercepts the summary timer without modifying the CC binary. It identifies the timer callback by source-text anchors and leaves other timers alone.

In controlled tests on Linux (from ver 2.1.257 to 2.1.312), the same workload produced five summary calls without the hook and zero with suppression enabled. On our current production setup, agent_summary calls remained at zero with the hook enabled. Background agents and forks continued running. The only visible change was that their generated status summaries stopped updating.

The workaround depends on implementation details. An update can break the callback matching and silently restore the requests. macOS and Windows are untested. If someone could help us with testing there, it would be much appreciated.

If you want to try it - the script, full technical explanation, test results, and installation instructions are on GitHub: https://gist.github.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa...

comment_text.value:
Aside from the opus5.5/fable + sub-lockin arguement...

Building an exceptional harness requires exceptional understanding of the technology you are harnessing.

Ant is building Claude Code in a place of frontier knowledge and advancement - everything surrounding the tool at Anthropic is something that does not exist within any "open source" organization. OC has recruited exceptional developer and new-media talent, but they have largely developed from a "catchup/copy" and designer-led process, and have consistently been behind in terms of capabilities and/or have misaligned implementation due to what I would classify as disadvantages of not understanding the underlying technology fully. I think this has led to a lot of unintended bloat - maintaining a plugin for it has been consistently very head-scratching experience.

- Pi was a refreshing welcome to the OSS arena with thoughtful design to enable simplicity and ecosystem-based development

In October 2026 - Claude Code feels further stretched ahead. The orchestration/projects model you get with sub agents either in the cloud/remote or local is the strongest capability I have experienced in awhile. Beyond the model intelligence the harness has been consistently refined and now includes things like Mods for robust customization. OC is pushing through big milestone release, not advancing on the front in terms of agentic engineering ux. Who came up with MCP, Slack/Claude Tag interface paradigm (less about slack), dynamic workflows, durable subagents, agent-to-agent communication across the harness, etc

comment_text.value:
> When you hear about the work Anthropic researchers are doing, they seem to be using hundreds or thousands of agents to solve problems.

There's a reason they're Anthropic researchers. The value proposition tanks when you actually have to foot the bill for the tokens you use.

Subagent flows can improve overall performance, but it generally also comes with disproportionately high token use. That gets worse with parallel subagents that are often doing the same things at the same time and cannot share a cache.

comment_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Colin. I built Parley so that multiple coding-agents using different models or harnesses can collaborate over a live IRC channel, with me in the chat using any IRC client. Each session can deliver messages to the channel using the `parley send` CLI tool call and sessions receive messages using their harnesses' channel or queue interface. All messages received on the channel are marked as coming from a peer so a session can never take another agent's message as coming from me. It works on Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode.

Parley is a standalone Go CLI, stdlib only, Apache 2.0. It runs its own ergo IRC server on 127.0.0.1 (loopback only), so nothing touches a public network. I built it with Claude Code and Codex.

The motivation came from wanting to explore a more interactive collaboration structure between agents rather than a simple sub-agent delegation model. It allows running multiple long-running agents with assigned roles which I provide as their first message in the chat. My typical setup so far assigns a builder role to execute build and review tasks, a planner role to supervise the overall goal, task ordering, and scheduling and an ops role to handle everything related to infrastructure, operations, deployments, secops, etc. All 3 can now interactively update/sync each other at every turn and start collaborating across their roles. There is a configurable breaker to pause the session until I post if there are too many messages in a short window.

I use it on macOS; on Linux the test suite passes in CI but I haven't run it live.

https://github.com/colinsurprenant/parley#what-a-line-looks-...

comment_text.value:
This is what we as consumers should look out for; what the tools built on top of LLMs try to do. Like it's neat that a tool can summon a dozen subagents with various models to churn out tasks, but if the task at hand is trivial then the amount of tokens used for it should be trivial.

We'll see the tools get adjusted over time to use more and more tokens, or at the very least they get optimized to use every paying customer's tokens for whatever period so that they are on the one side thinking they're getting their money's worth, or on the other that they should upgrade to a higher tier plan. Because the companies are investing trillions into thousands of datacenters and if they sit unused it'd have been a waste of money.

(the datacenters won't go unused I'm sure; any unused capacity will end up on a spot market, with cryptocurrency generation as a constant baseline. I'm pretty confident that crypto will make another small resurgence after the AI / datacenter investment bubble pops. This is a random internet comment, not financial advice)

Glancing over the methodology[1] made me curious about three things:

1. Is there a benchmark measuring how much better an LLM performs when you tell it "you are an X"?

comment_text.value:
Hello, everyone. A friend of mine wanted to get into running local models, and so (with the liberal use of Claude), I built them Zest.

https://github.com/yudhanjaya/Zest

What it is:

Zest is a UI that bundles Lemonade server (which installs llama.cpp and whatever backends are needed) and the Pi agent to provide a friendly interface for people who don't want to be messing around with command-line servers and parameters.

It comes and all the functionality needed for a new user without getting in the way. Just download an appimage, go through the start tour, and you're set up and ready to go. There are sane defaults baked in (like 128k context) and model recommendations (all tried and tested on 10GB VRAM to 26GB).

r/LocalLLaMA - Introducing Zest: model server + agent + friendly GUI It comes with helpful docs, links to places to understand more about the subject - in short, everything needed for a new user. Model recommendations are based on my own testing on multiple machines with consumer GPUs - an old Xeon with two Radeon VIIs, a rig with a 4080 Super + a 3080, a rig with a venerable 1080. The goal is to present good choices for most hardware.

Entirely open-source, of course. If you have anyone you want to introduce to the world of local AI, please see if this is useful. And if you have ideas, suggestions - please open an issue, send a PR, and so on.

Why lemonade and Pi?

Lemonade: because it does a great job of handling backends and providing a server.

Pi: because it's a simple, elegant agent

Both are very easy to package in something like this and bring together. And because I'm lazy: both projects are receiving steady updates, because I don't want to write yet another inference server from scratch

What it isn't:

It's not for advanced users. There are jobs, but no subagents, for instance: in this case the Pi philosophy really helped.

In fact, I myself use Strata and Opencode, so for advanced users, it recommends those in the Help section

How is this different from Unsloth desktop / Atomic chat etc?

It isn't. It just tries to be a lot more lightweight and user-friendly: I decided to do this after getting said friend to download and set up llama.cpp, Unsloth Desktop, Opencode etc . . .

I noticed that at some point both choice paralysis and confusion with options just took over, and there was no easy way for them as a newcomer to figure out what x thing was really for. Every setting in Zest is explained. Including what inference engines do, the works.

Everything is explained at basic levels - what a model is, how it works, and so on. I've kept the lemonade + pi analogy while trying to make sure the interface was intuitive.

story_title.value: Friendly UI and server and agent for local LLMs

comment_text.value:
> Related thing is that LLMs are still notoriously bad at writing instructions for themselves (so managing themselves also).

Isn't this odd? This seems to be the #1 task that the major labs should be optimizing, since it makes agent so much more effective.

> They tend to overspecify. If I had a copy of myself I would tell him "do the thing", but agents say "do the thing like this and this, it must be such and such, use X and put it together that way". The subagent is just as intelligent but now it's constrained, sometimes as you start developing something you discover some things are better organized in a different way etc. So it spends much time figuring out how to deliver exactly what was asked even if it's not optimal because that's the task.

Isn't this just the planning pattern, common for agentic work? (first plan then implement.. with things like /plan, or a planning skill, with or without creating a PLAN.md). If this methodology is wrong when an agent prompt another agent, it's also wrong when the human runs /plan manually..

And Indeed, I always thought it was odd to constrain the implementing agent like that, because common sense is that we discover things as we implement. Perhaps we should prompt the agent to communicate back, as they implement, any shortcomings in the plan itself - such as things they learned while implementing that contradicts the plan.

Related thing is that LLMs are still notoriously bad at writing instructions for themselves (so managing themselves also). They tend to overspecify. If I had a copy of myself I would tell him "do the thing", but agents say "do the thing like this and this, it must be such and such, use X and put it together that way". The subagent is just as intelligent but now it's constrained, sometimes as you start developing something you discover some things are better organized in a different way etc. So it spends much time figuring out how to deliver exactly what was asked even if it's not optimal because that's the task.

Basically a company where you can't ever question decisions of the higher ups, not even ask for clarification, but they force implementation choices on you. I mean, it definitely does happen, but the results are usually not great. Not alawys. For some tasks it works.

The subagent is just as intelligent but now it's constrained, sometimes as you start developing something you discover some things are better organized in a different way etc. So it spends much time figuring out how to deliver exactly what was asked even if it's not optimal because that's the task.

Basically a company where you can't ever question decisions of the higher ups, not even ask for clarification, but they force implementation choices on you. I mean, it definitely does happen, but the results are usually not great. Not alawys. For some tasks it works.

comment_text.value:
It's a weird way to express that concept, in fact I don't think it ever appeared like this in the book (it has been a while).

It would be something like "nine women cannot deliver a baby in one month", which can be more easily transposed to "adding resources to a SW project does not make it faster".

The agrument is that adding people increase coordination and communication overhead, which gets bigger as the team grows. Moreover, some tasks cannot be parallelized that easily and create dependencies.

I have only worked with agents for personal projects, but I cannot say that explicity dividing the work between multiple agents and asking them to coordinate is inherently faster than having a single agent work on it (of course the single agent will spawn subagents in rencent harnesses.)

comment_text.value:
I'm using OMP (oh-my-pi) and the minimum you need to do is just set the @task role to Deepseek:max.

Subagents can spawn with other profiles e.g. scout (uses @smol) and reviewer (@slow). You can set SOTA with higher thinking for @slow and Deepseek with lower thinking for @smol or something even faster/cheaper.

There's also weirdly named /vibe mode that gives explicit instructions to the main model to act as an orchestrator but I find this unnecessary if your main is SOTA, they are already super eager to spawn subagents by default.
